title: Mostly quiet
hook: speak rarely and only what's needed, and not about people (Enchiridion 33)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the diviner, and the one question you never need to ask. Your line was reason has already answered. Which duty did you do without waiting? Day three hundred sixty-five.

Three hundred sixty-five. A whole calendar's worth of days. Worth one breath of its own. Now, a test. Think back over yesterday's conversations, every one of them, the kitchen, the office, the group chat. How many were about someone who wasn't there? It's not a trick question, and the answer can be a little uncomfortable. The handbook's thirty-third section is a long one, a set of small rules for how a person of character talks, laughs and listens. We'll take it over a few days. It starts with the mouth. Today: mostly quiet.
screen: `THREE HUNDRED SIXTY-FIVE.` → `HOW MUCH TALK WAS ABOUT SOMEONE ELSE?` → `MOSTLY QUIET.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. Section thirty-three begins: decide now on a certain character and pattern for yourself, and keep to it, whether you're alone or with other people. Everything after is a sketch of that character. Second, the first stroke of the sketch. Let silence be the general rule, Epictetus says. Or say only what's needed, and in few words. That's not a vow of silence. It's a default, like a resting position. Third, what to skip when you do talk. Rarely, when the moment calls for it, speak, he says, but not about the ordinary topics: gladiators, horse races, athletes, food and drink. Those were the everyday topics of his world, he implies. Translate them into today and you'll recognize the list. Epictetus isn't banning sports. He's noticing how many hours of a life can go into conversation that leaves nobody changed. Fourth, and above all, not about people. Don't blame them, he says, don't praise them, don't compare them. That's the one he leans on hardest. And then a gentler line: if you can, turn your friends' conversation toward something worthwhile, and if you find yourself among strangers, keep quiet. Why would a Stoic care so much? Because talk about absent people is almost always talk about things outside our control: what they did, what they're like, what they deserve. It feeds judgment and envy, and it rarely helps the person being discussed. Mostly quiet isn't cold. It leaves room for the conversations that matter.
screen: `CHOOSE A CHARACTER, AND KEEP IT.` · `SILENCE AS THE DEFAULT.` · `SKIP THE GLADIATORS AND HORSE RACES.` · `ABOVE ALL, NOT ABOUT PEOPLE.` · then, large: `MOSTLY QUIET.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Let the noise of the day thin out. Now picture the moment, later today, when a conversation turns toward someone who isn't there. There may be a pull to it, the little thrill of the story. See yourself letting it pass. Maybe you say nothing. Maybe you ask the other person how they're doing instead. Notice what it feels like not to add a word. Then just rest in the quiet you're sitting in now. The bell holds the time.
Mostly quiet. Epictetus' first rule for a person of character: silence by default, few words when needed, and not about people. Today's word.
Your line: let silence be the rule. When talk turns to someone who isn't there today, skip one piece of gossip. Let it pass, or change the subject. Day three hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Some people who practice Stoicism treat silence as their default in conversation and make a habit of not discussing absent people, especially not blaming, praising or comparing them.

myth: Epictetus asks for a total vow of silence
silence is the general rule; speak when needed, in few words.
he warns against praising absent people, not just blaming them
blaming, praising and comparing are all on his list.

fork.setup: you're with friends and the talk turns to an absent coworker. what does Epictetus suggest?
options: if you can, turn the talk toward something worthwhile.
fork.reveal: he says to turn friends' conversation toward what's fitting if you can, and among strangers simply to keep quiet.

original.note: Greek: silence, which Enchiridion 33 makes the general rule.

trapdoor: what you thought: Stoics were just strong and silent types.
what it means: silence is a default, few words when needed, and above all no talk that blames, praises or compares people.
what a scholar hears: section thirty-three, a long run of small rules, opens by asking you to choose a character and keep it, alone or in company.

notes: Review (2026-10-01): cut 'most people don't love the answer', 'one of its longest' (twice) and 'the small talk of Rome'; the practice no longer tells the listener what they feel.

Enchiridion 33.1–3 paraphrased: prescribe a character and pattern; silence for the most part, or only what is necessary in few words; speak rarely, not about gladiators, horse races, athletes, food, drink; above all not about men, blaming, praising or comparing; bring friends' talk to what is fitting; among strangers be silent. Confirm.
'One of its longest' for section 33: confirm.
Greek σιωπή: confirm it appears in Ench. 33.2 and the pronunciation.
